about.title: Morgan Hill Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Morgan Hill's mix of downtown storefronts, shopping plazas near US-101, and busy corridors like Monterey Road and Dunne Avenue means residents regularly move through properties owned by someone else — grocery stores, restaurants, apartment complexes, parking lots. When a wet floor, broken step, uneven pavement, or poor lighting causes a fall, California law asks whether the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and failed to address it. That question often turns on details: how long a spill sat there, whether a mat was missing, what a surveillance camera captured. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we're a free service that connects injured Morgan Hill residents with an independent attorney who can evaluate the notice issue, gather evidence before it disappears, and explain your options. There's no cost to get connected, and attorneys in this network work on contingency, meaning no fee unless you recover something.

whyChoose.title: Why Notice and Timing Matter in a Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California premises law doesn't automatically hold an owner responsible just because you fell — you generally need to show they had notice of the hazard and didn't fix or warn about it. An attorney can help identify what evidence supports that notice, from maintenance logs to prior complaints.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many stores and apartment complexes overwrite security footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having video evidence and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: Even if a property owner argues you weren't watching where you stepped, California's pure comparative fault rule means your claim isn't automatically barred — any shared fault reduces recovery rather than eliminating it.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Morgan Hill?
items.answer: In general, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit for a premises liability injury. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as a city building or a park, that deadline is much shorter and requires an earlier claim filing. An attorney can confirm which timeline applies to your situation.

items.question: I fell at a store near Monterey Road but didn't take photos — is my claim over?
items.answer: No, but acting quickly helps. Store surveillance cameras, incident reports the business may have filed, and witness accounts can still support your case even without your own photos. An attorney can send a request to preserve video before it's deleted.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for not seeing the hazard?
items.answer: California follows a pure comparative fault rule, so being partially responsible doesn't automatically prevent you from recovering compensation. Instead, any fault attributed to you would reduce the amount you might recover. This is a fact-specific question best discussed with an attorney familiar with your circumstances.
